props.title: Day of Wrath
props.initialSlug: A widow faces witchcraft accusations in Puritan Denmark

sections.content: Carl Theodor Dreyer's Day of Wrath (1943) stands as one of cinema's most haunting examinations of religious hysteria and persecution. Shot during the Nazi occupation of Denmark, the film's exploration of witch hunts in 17th-century Denmark carries clear parallels to contemporary fascism. Dreyer's methodical pacing and use of stark black-and-white photography creates an atmosphere of mounting dread that influenced later psychological horror, from The Witch (2015) to Mother! (2017). The story of young Anne, married to an elderly pastor while falling in love with his son, interweaves forbidden desire with themes of institutional power and mob mentality.

sections.content: Dreyer's visual style in Day of Wrath revolutionized how cinema could capture interior psychological states. His use of slow, creeping camera movements and extreme close-ups of faces in spiritual torment influenced directors like Ingmar Bergman, particularly in Winter Light (1963) and The Silence (1963). The film's exploration of generational conflict and sexual repression through the lens of religious authority created a template for later works like The Devils (1971) and The Crucible (1996).

The film's treatment of witch hunts resonates deeply with contemporary witch-themed cinema, from The Craft (1996) to Suspiria (2018). But where modern films often position witchcraft as female empowerment, Day of Wrath focuses on how religious authority weaponizes accusations of witchcraft to maintain control. This approach influenced serious historical examinations like The Witch (2015) and Black Sunday (1960). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence on Religious Cinema

sections.content: The film's impact extends beyond witch-hunt narratives into broader religious cinema. Its unflinching look at faith, doubt, and human cruelty laid groundwork for films like Silence (2016) and First Reformed (2017). Dreyer's ability to make spiritual struggles visually compelling influenced Paul Schrader's entire career, from Mishima: A Life in Four Chapters (1985) to his recent work.
